title: Joanna Wiebe (Copyhackers), Attention Interest Desire Action (AIDA)
text:
## AIDA: the oldest conversion sequence

AIDA stands for Attention, Interest, Desire, Action. It maps the reader's journey from first noticing your message to taking the one next step you want. Copyhackers frames each stage as a job the copy must do in order.

## The four stages, defined

Attention: using a stellar headline, tell your reader what they are looking for and why they should want it. Copyhackers stresses that headlines carry disproportionate weight, roughly five times as many people read your headline as read your body copy, so the Attention stage is where most of the win or loss happens.

Interest: show potential customers why your product is fantastic using facts to engage their minds. Interest is the rational hook, evidence and specifics that make the reader lean in.

Desire: show your prospective customer how life will be different after using this product. Find that deep emotional benefit. Desire is the emotional shift, the after state the reader wants.

Action: give your target market a clear way they can take the next step, but only ONE next step. Multiple competing calls to action dilute response.

## Refinements a pro makes

You do not have to play hard and fast with this formula. In real copy Interest and Desire blend together, and a single long page can repeat the AIDA cycle several times rather than run through it once linearly. Apple's copy is cited as an example where interest and desire fuse.

## Critical guidance

Headlines must avoid clickbait tactics like excessive caps, the word FREE, and false claims. Never present multiple call to action options, provide one clear next step. Precede any copywriting with voice of customer research so each AIDA stage is filled with the reader's own words rather than your assumptions. The working method: start with VOC research, pour findings into the AIDA sections, draft, edit, then elevate the headline and CTA last.

title: Bob Bly, The Motivating Sequence (via Copy Engineer)
text:
## The Motivating Sequence

Bob Bly, often called the dean of business to business copywriters, teaches a five step structure he calls the Motivating Sequence. It is a practical variation on AIDA and gives long copy promotions (sales letters, landing pages) a reliable skeleton. A memory aid for the order is APSPA: Attention, Problem, Solution, Proof, Action.

## Step 1: Attention

Gain the prospect's attention. This is usually the headline's job: identify your target reader and communicate a benefit relevant to them so the right person keeps reading.

## Step 2: Interest / Problem

Engage the reader's interest by identifying a problem the reader has or a need that must be filled. Keep this brief, just enough to prove you understand their challenge and that the message is about them.

## Step 3: Solution

Position your product, service, or company as the solution to the reader's problem. This often needs only a short transition statement that connects the problem to what you sell.

## Step 4: Proof

Offer proof to convince skeptical readers that your claim to solve their problem is true. Proof comes from credentials, testimonials, case histories, research results, client lists, plus awards, licenses, degrees, certifications, affiliations, and other demonstrations of your reputation, expertise, and stability.

## Step 5: Action

Invite the reader to take action toward implementing your solution. This might be to request more information or to order the product or service. Include a clear reply mechanism and avoid weak closings.

## Why it works

Business readers want information that solves their problems and improves their productivity. By answering What's in it for me upfront, then proving it, the sequence captures attention and walks the prospect toward a response.

title: Gary Bencivenga, 5 Powerful Copywriting Tips (via Jeremy Mac)
text:
## Gary Bencivenga, five principles

Gary Bencivenga is widely regarded as one of the greatest direct response copywriters. These five principles distill his approach.

## 1. The power of metaphors

Use metaphors to make an idea instantly understandable. The formula is the point you are trying to make plus a metaphor. A metaphor taps into the reader's mind faster than a direct statement, so the reader is both entertained and persuaded.

## 2. The red shirts phenomenon

Train your attention on what you want to achieve. When you focus on something you begin to notice it everywhere. Scan daily for marketing ideas, stories, and persuasive hooks in ads, emails, and media, so your mind becomes a magnet for usable material.

## 3. The secret of how to sell anything

Find out what others want and help them get it. Write exclusively for your target audience's desires, not your own preferences. Research what the market actually wants, then persuade them to try (rather than buy) your offering.

## 4. A gifted product is mightier than a gifted pen

Great copy cannot compensate for an inferior product. There must be an already existing demand for what you sell. Writing for a red hot market that is starving for your product makes success nearly automatic. This echoes Gary Halbert's starving crowd: the market matters more than the words.

## 5. Because

Always give the reason why after a claim. The word because acts as a psychological trigger that lowers skepticism, an effect supported by Robert Cialdini's research. Reasons make claims believable and persuasive.

title: Gary Bencivenga, What Are We Really Selling (via Story Power Marketing)
text:
## The most important advertising question

Gary Bencivenga taught that before writing a word, you must answer one question: what are we really selling? Successful copy sells the underlying benefit or aspiration, not the physical product or its features.

## Sell the result, not the thing

Bencivenga's examples make the distinction concrete. You are not selling grass seed, you are selling a greener lawn. You are not selling boilers and BTUs, you are selling warmer, cozier winter nights at a 27 percent fuel savings. You are not selling baseball tickets, you are selling memories of sunny afternoons that a father and his children will cherish forever.

## The classic parallel

The same idea appears in Charles Revson's line about his cosmetics company: in the factory we make cosmetics, in the store we sell hope. The lesson for a copywriter: translate every feature into the deeper human outcome the reader actually wants, then lead with that outcome.

title: Joanna Wiebe (Copyhackers), Find Your Message Using Review Mining
text:
## Do not create the message, steal it from your prospects

The core principle of conversion copywriting is that you do not invent messaging from your own perspective. You extract the language directly from customer feedback and use it, close to verbatim, in your copy.

## Four questions before you mine

Answer these in order first: who is my target audience, what solutions do I believe they want, what solutions might they be using today, and if those solutions are online, where are they.

## The review mining method

Identify relevant products or services your prospects currently use. Locate reviews on platforms like Amazon, TripAdvisor, or app stores. Read through the reviews systematically. Extract customer language verbatim into a categorized table. Organize the findings into three buckets: loves, hates, and worries. Then identify recurring themes and standout phrases. For the Beachway rehab example this meant reading 500 plus reviews across 6 addiction related books on Amazon.

## The Beachway rehab case study

Mining those 500 plus reviews surfaced a phrase in the reviewers' own words. The winning headline, taken from customer language, was: If you think you need rehab, you do. The control headline was: Your Addiction Ends Here.

Results of the test: a 400 percent increase in clicks on the call to action button, and a 20 percent increase in lead generation form submissions on the next page. This customer sourced headline outperformed every subsequent treatment tested against it. The lesson: your best headline is often already written by your customers, you just have to find it.

title: Copyhackers, 7 Copywriting Research Techniques for Voice of Customer
text:
## Research is where copy is won

Conversion copywriters do not start by writing. They start by researching, because research reveals both the messaging hierarchy (the order the messages go in) and the exact words to say. These seven techniques gather voice of customer data.

## 1. Client and customer interviews

Live, come as you are conversations with clients, their teams, current customers, and former customers. Use open ended questions and dig deeper on interesting answers. Described as the number one best way to get unfiltered language and the sticky messages every copywriter needs.

## 2. Surveys

Structured questionnaires to visitors and customers that surface usage scenarios, outcomes, objections, anxieties, decision influencers, financial impact, and quality of life improvements.

## 3. Review mining

Analysis of online reviews on Amazon, Reddit, Yelp, TripAdvisor and similar, where prospects discuss products like yours. Captures unfiltered opinions and the search terminology prospects actually use.

## 4. Heatmaps and scrollmaps

Visual behavior tools like Hotjar. Click heatmaps show which links pull attention, scroll heatmaps show how far people read so you can place key content where it will be seen.

## 5. Thank you polls

Post conversion micro surveys deployed right after an opt in or purchase, asking a single question about what prompted the action, revealing the primary motivation.

## 6. Analytics review

Traffic sources, session duration, conversion rates, and goal alignment, to understand behavior and where copy is leaking.

## 7. Competitor audits

Examine direct and indirect competitors' messaging, positioning, and objection handling to find differentiation and positioning gaps.

## The messy middle

Between gathering the data and outlining the copy sits the work of consolidating it into a messaging hierarchy. Do this before you write a line.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Microcontent: How to Write Headlines, Page Titles, and Subject Lines
text:
## What microcontent is

Microcontent is a type of UX copywriting made of short text fragments or phrases, often shown with no additional context: headlines, page titles, email subject lines, link labels. Because it frequently appears out of context in feeds, search results, and inboxes, it must work on its own.

## Core principles

Write in plain language and avoid puns and clever wording. Remove nonessential words to improve scannability. Move the keywords to the front so the item supports attention and scanning. The microcontent must deliver good content, keep interest alive, and provide value, not just tease.

## Page titles

Optimal length is 40 to 60 characters. Include keywords that boost the content's ranking. Omit leading articles like the and a. Front load keywords for both search visibility and human scanning.

## Headlines

Make sure the headline works out of context, because it will appear in feeds and on social media detached from the page. Tell readers something useful, be specific rather than generic. Avoid clickbait and teasers that do not deliver on their promise.

## Email subject lines

Be concise and start with keywords. Address the user's benefit and actual need. Clearly explain what the email is about in terms that relate to the user. The recurring rule across all microcontent: specificity and front loading beat vague, generic, or clever language, because users scan with limited attention.

title: The 4 Ps Formula: Promise, Picture, Proof, Push (via GMass)
text:
## The 4 Ps: Promise, Picture, Proof, Push

The 4 Ps is a four part persuasion structure well suited to long form sales pages, product descriptions, and email. It leads with a benefit, makes it vivid, proves it, then drives action.

## Promise

A big benefit you are offering to a prospect that makes them stop and take notice. Diagnose the recipient's pain point, speak directly to it, and deliver an eye catching solution with an economy of words. The promise is the headline level hook.

## Picture

Vividly describe what the prospect's life will look like after implementing the solution. Use storytelling to evoke an emotional response rather than listing features. This is the after state made tangible.

## Proof

Hard numbers or evidence backing up why they should believe you can make the promise come true. Use case studies, testimonials, statistics, or social proof to overcome objections through logic. Proof answers the skeptic.

## Push

An aggressive call to action. Make a strong appeal that drives immediate action, often adding urgency or scarcity. The push converts interest into a decision.

## Note

A closely related AWAI variant expands the picture step as Paint a Picture using metaphors, stories, and analogies to bring the problem and solution to life, then Promise, Provide Proof, and Push for Response with a highly desirable, hard to refuse offer.

title: Joanna Wiebe (Copyhackers), How to Optimize Your Button Copy
text:
## Buttons are conversion critical

You cannot convert online without clicking one or more buttons, so button copy deserves deliberate crafting, not a default label. The single most useful distinction is calls to value versus calls to action.

## Calls to value (top of funnel)

Before the prospect has decided to buy, a call to value amplifies the value of clicking. Write it so it completes the phrase I want to [benefit], and put it in first person voice. Examples: be my own boss, get my free inspection, customize my palette, show me how, grow my audience, end my accounting hassles, show me my quiz results. It should feel effortless and desirable, focused on the outcome, not the technical action.

## Calls to action (bottom of funnel)

As the prospect approaches purchase and needs clarity on what happens next, describe the specific action: buy now, add to cart, complete booking, complete purchase. These are explicit and UX focused, appropriate only at the final decision point.

## Key rules

Minimize perceived work: even the tiniest idea of work, even a little extra pinch of work, will reduce your conversion rate on a button. Avoid scary language: buying is a scary word, so minimize terms that imply effort like buy, sign up, and learn until the reader is ready. Optimize your primary CTA and deliberately de optimize secondary ones: on a pricing page, use friction heavy language for the paths you do not want, and reserve the optimized, value framed copy for your preferred route. Match the funnel: value focused copy earlier, action focused copy only at the end.

title: Copyblogger, Three Enemies of Clear and Direct Writing (anti-pattern)
text:
## Clarity first: three enemies to kill

Unclear copy does not persuade. Copyblogger names three specific enemies of clear, direct writing that copywriters must hunt down and remove.

## Enemy 1: Metadiscourse

Writing about your writing, which is almost always extraneous. Avoid phrases like to sum up, candidly, I believe, note that, it has become clear, and I would like to point out. The fix: cut the commentary about what you are saying and just say it. Instead of I would like to take this opportunity to extend to you a hearty congratulations, write Congratulations.

## Enemy 2: Redundancy

Using more words than needed via repetitive modifiers. Avoid screaming loudly (screaming already implies loud), your own personal cubicle (all three words say the same thing), MLB Baseball (the abbreviation already contains baseball), and past history (history is already past). The fix: see what a word already conveys and delete the duplicate descriptor, choose one word that stands alone.

## Enemy 3: Pretentious words

Picking obscure, impressive sounding vocabulary instead of the simple word the broad audience understands. Replace inexorable with determined or unstoppable, utilize with use, ameliorate with improve, clandestine with secret or hidden, comprehend with understand. The fix: prioritize clarity and accessibility over sounding sophisticated. Your goal is to inform your reader, not to impress them.

title: Joanna Wiebe (Copyhackers), How to Write a Long Form Sales Page
text:
## Research before writing

Before drafting a long form sales page, run a scavenger hunt for sticky messages: gather voice of customer data from internal sources (analytics, past surveys, chat transcripts), external sources (testimonials, social mentions, competitor analysis), client interviews, and product testing. Organize it in a template that separates FAQs, quotes, testimonials, and sticky messages by the section they will feed. All messaging is derived from VoC data, not guessing.

## The page flow (a PAS backbone)

Trust and credibility: establish credentials, media mentions, and user numbers early.

Problem: open with a pain point the reader recognizes, in the customer's own language, exactly what people said about themselves.

Agitation: deepen the problem and show its cascading consequences, addressing the root cause (for example, diets do not work) and the emotional stakes. This is also where the it is not your fault framing lives: previous solutions failed the reader in important ways.

Solution: introduce your approach as different or new, with an origin story and the research behind it, to build trust in the method.

Product: show ease of use via screenshots, illustrate the transformation across days, weeks, and months, and show how it fits the reader's life.

Supporting elements: video testimonials carrying sticky messages, written testimonials (the strongest saved for the close), and FAQs that answer objections.

Close: reveal the price with minimal framing (only X per month), a strong call to action paired with a risk reversal guarantee, and a powerful closing testimonial.

## Practical rules

Break each main statement into supporting statements and turn them into crossheads so skimmers can read the page by subheads alone. Present the outline or wireframe for approval before writing full copy. A long form page works because it captures the complete customer journey on a single page.

title: Alex Hormozi on Guarantees and Risk Reversal (via Shortform)
text:
## Risk reversal: remove the fear of buying

Risk is a major point of sales friction. A guarantee shifts risk from the customer to the business, which lowers purchase resistance and signals genuine confidence in the product. As a way of saying we believe in our product so much we are willing to back it up, a strong guarantee can raise closing rates and net revenue even if refunds rise slightly.

## Type 1: Unconditional guarantee

A straightforward promise: satisfaction or your money back within a specific period. No conditions on the buyer. This is the boldest and most trust building form.

## Type 2: Conditional guarantee

The refund depends on the customer meeting certain criteria or completing certain actions. For example, a refund only if the client is not satisfied after attending all the sessions in the program, or show up three times a week and log your meals, and if you do not get the result, full refund. Conditional guarantees also nudge the behavior that makes success likely.

## Type 3: Outcome based guarantee

Tied to the customer achieving a result. For example, a consultant who does not charge upfront but takes a commission once the customer reaches the desired outcome. The seller is paid on performance.

## The copywriting takeaway

Name the guarantee boldly and put it near the offer and the call to action. A specific, vivid guarantee (with a name and a clear promise) reverses the reader's risk at the exact moment of decision and outperforms a vague or buried refund policy.

title: Joseph Sugarman, The Adweek Copywriting Handbook: Slippery Slide and First Sentence (via Jeremy Mac)
text:
## The slippery slide

Joseph Sugarman's central image is the slippery slide: once a reader starts, the copy should carry them from headline to conclusion effortlessly, with no friction to grab onto. You grease the slide with short sentences, short paragraphs, and short words, plus engaging stories, strategic subheadings, and sensory details that keep the momentum going.

## The purpose of every graphic element

Sugarman lists ten elements of an ad: headline, sub headline, photo, caption, copy, paragraph headings, logo, price, response device, and layout. Every one of them shares a single objective: to get you to read the first sentence of the copy. Nothing on the page exists for its own sake, each element earns its place only by pulling the eye toward that first line.

## The sole purpose of the first sentence

Each sentence has one job: to get the reader to read the next sentence. The headline's job is to get the first sentence read, the first sentence's job is to get the second read, and so on down the slide until the reader reaches the call to action. This simplifies writing: you are never trying to sell in one line, only to earn the next line. Sugarman greases the transitions with seeds of curiosity, short connectors like But there's more, So read on, and Let me explain.

## The incubation process

After research and between drafts, step away and let the subconscious work through exercise, social time, or other activity. Breakthrough ideas often surface during these breaks, so capture them immediately.

## Honesty and proof

The most powerful emotional trigger is truthfulness. Support every claim with social proof (testimonials, reviews) and specific detail. As Gary Bencivenga advises, never make your claims bigger than your proof.

title: Donald Miller, Building a StoryBrand: the SB7 Framework (via Shortform)
text:
## The customer is the hero, not your brand

The biggest reframe in Donald Miller's StoryBrand is who the hero is. Most companies cast themselves as the impressive, decades of experience hero. Miller's rule: cast the customer as the hero and cast your brand as the guide. The only thing customers care about is how your brand can solve their problems. Marketing fails when it is confusing, overwhelming, narcissistic, or takes too much energy to understand. The governing law is: if you confuse, you lose.

## The SB7 framework, seven elements in order

1. A Character. The customer is the hero and wants something. Start by naming what the hero wants.

2. Has a Problem. The customer hits a problem that stops them from getting it. Miller splits it three ways: the external problem (the tangible obstacle), the internal problem (how it makes them feel), and the philosophical problem (why it is just plain wrong). Copy that speaks to the internal problem outperforms copy that only names the external one.

3. Meets a Guide. Your brand enters as the guide, showing two things: empathy (we understand your pain) and authority (we have the competence to help).

4. Who gives them a Plan. A clear, simple, actionable set of steps that removes the fear of doing business with you.

5. And calls them to Action. Direct calls to action (buy now, schedule a call) and transitional calls to action (download the guide) that invite the hero to move.

6. That helps them avoid Failure. Make the stakes clear: what the hero stands to lose if they do not act. Without stakes, there is no story.

7. And ends in Success. Show the hero what life looks like after they win, the positive transformation your product makes possible.

## Why it works for copy

Run any homepage or sales page through SB7 and it strips the message down to the seven story elements the brain is already built to follow, which is why the customer keeps reading and knows exactly what to do next.

title: Copywriter Collective, Write to One Reader (anti-pattern: writing to everyone)
text:
## The anti-pattern: writing to everyone

A classic copywriting mistake is trying to appeal to everyone at once. When you write to a broad audience, the copy becomes impersonal and forgettable. It communicates information without creating a connection, describing benefits without touching the emotional reality of the reader's life. Generic messaging lacks resonance.

## The single reader principle

Your sales message needs to speak to one person and one person only. Write your copy directly to that person, and that person alone, and it becomes more direct and personal. The guiding maxim: write to somebody well rather than to many people badly.

## Build a real avatar, not a demographic sketch

Surface demographics (Sandra, 36, from London) do not actually guide the writing. A useful avatar goes deeper into psychographics: what their day actually feels like, their emotional state in specific situations, and the decision making constraints they face. For example, a comms manager who joined the charity only a few months ago is not just a fact, it signals she might feel a little out of her depth, which shapes how you pitch to her.

## The you orientation

Writing to one person is genuine empathy in practice. You are not guessing, you are responding to a specific person's actual circumstances, which produces copy in the second person (you) that speaks directly to their needs and fears.

title: Copyhackers, Advanced Email Copywriting: Subject Line Triggers
text:
## Four psychological triggers for subject lines

Copyhackers grounds subject line writing in four evidence based triggers. Salience: standing out visually in a crowded inbox. Personalization: tailoring to the individual subscriber. Curiosity: creating intrigue without revealing the answer. Scarcity: conveying limited availability or time sensitivity. A strong subject line usually leans on one of these, not all four at once.

## Conversational tone wins

Informal, friend to friend language outperforms polished marketing language. The Obama campaign famously won with the subject line hey, showing that simplicity often beats complexity. Write the way you would to a friend.

## Visual distinctiveness

Beyond keeping it short, you can make a subject line stand out with numbers, symbols, the occasional emoji, or unusual formatting, so it catches the eye while scanning.

## Avoid the curiosity gap trap

A critical mistake: the preview text reveals what the subject line teased. That eliminates the reason to open. If the subject line opens a loop, the preview text must not close it.

## Do not repeat past formulas

Subject lines lose effectiveness when reused. What worked last quarter fatigues, so continuous testing and fresh approaches beat formula repetition. Keep them short enough to display fully on mobile, where most opens happen.

title: Copyhackers, How to Write Emails: The Conversion Copywriter's Approach
text:
## A three stage process

Conversion email writing follows Research and Discovery, then Draft and Format, then Validate and Experiment. Effective email is a research backed strategy, not spontaneous composition: you are not the problem, you just need a process.

## The subject line's one job

The subject line's number one job is to get the reader to open your email. Create at least 50 subject line variations using voice of customer data, then pick and test.

## Meet the reader's awareness

The opening line should engage readers where they currently stand in their awareness journey and move them toward conversion. Each email addresses a single clear objective aligned with the reader's stage of awareness: Unaware, Problem Aware, Solution Aware, Product Aware, or Most Aware.

## One idea, one CTA

Each message carries one idea and one clear call to action. Write the end first: establish your CTA before drafting the body so the whole email guides the reader toward one specific action.

## A persuasive structure

A reliable email structure is PAS, Problem, Agitation, Solution: name a specific problem, intensify the emotional response to it, then present your offer as the resolution. First line's job is to get the next line read, all the way to the single CTA.

title: Copyblogger, A Short Guide to Writing Good Copy
text:
## The goal: display window clear

Good copy sells without drawing attention to itself. As David Ogilvy put it, a good advertisement is one which sells the product without drawing attention to itself. These rules keep the writing invisible and the offer visible.

## The rules

Headline first: spend the majority of your effort on the headline, and make it pass the 4 Us, Useful, Urgent, Unique, and Ultra Specific.

Use common spelling: avoid cutesy variants like pleez, thru, nite, 2moro, that distract in longer copy.

Avoid hyperbole and fancy words: E B White advised do not be tempted by a twenty dollar word when there is a ten center handy.

Put the reader first: research your audience and use you, one of the most powerful words in English.

Write naturally: speak your audience's language as a real person offering genuine expertise, which builds know, like, and trust.

Work from an outline so you stay focused and do not ramble.

Write with nouns and verbs: precise language convinces, while adjectives and adverbs are often filler.

Revise and rewrite: Ogilvy edited first drafts four or five times before showing a client.

Do not overwrite, and do not overstate: understated promises capture attention better than exaggerated claims. This is the antidote to hype.

Be clear, do not mix metaphors, and simplify your language. As Strunk wrote, a sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, make every word tell.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, How Little Do Users Read? (why copy must be concise)
text:
## People do not read, they scan

A foundational fact every copywriter must internalize: online, users read at most 28 percent of the words during an average page visit, and 20 percent is more realistic. Assuming your copy earns any attention at all is a mistake. Only on very short pages of 111 words or fewer can users read about half of the content.

## The numbers behind it

The average page studied held 593 words. Users spend about 25 seconds on page layout and navigation, plus roughly 4.4 additional seconds per 100 words. At a reading speed of 250 words per minute, that works out to customers reading only about 18 percent of newly added text. The more words you add, the smaller the share that gets read. The finding comes from a 2005 naturalistic study by Weinreich and colleagues analyzing 45,237 cleaned page views.

## Implications for copy

Keep word counts minimal, especially for broad audiences. Front load the critical information, because users scan rather than read in order. Structure for scannability with headlines, lists, subheads, and white space. Every extra sentence competes for a share of attention that is already tiny, so cut anything that does not earn its place.
